# TUI — Theme, Colors & Background

### Rule 102 : Centralized management of colors and styles

- All colors must be defined in `internal/ui/theme/colors.go`
- Never hardcode colors directly in views
- Reusable styles must be defined in `internal/ui/theme/styles.go`
- Use the theme package's constants (ColorPrimary, ColorError, etc.)

### Rule 105 : Help message format

- Standard format: `[key] action  [key] action`
- Displayed with `theme.HelpStyle` (italic + ColorDim)
- Keys in square brackets `[]`
- Separated by at least 2 spaces

### Rule 115 : Uniform background handling (lipgloss)

With `app.theme: auto` the OSC 11 query comes before the theme's background: `View().BackgroundColor` stays `nil` while the detection is pending, so the terminal answers with its own color.

**lipgloss does NOT propagate a parent's background to its children.**

`JoinHorizontal`/`JoinVertical` insert "bare" spaces that show the terminal's native background.

| Forbidden | Alternative |
|----------|-------------|
| `lipgloss.JoinHorizontal` to assemble blocks | Build each line manually with `PadWithBg()` |
| `lipgloss.JoinVertical` to stack lines | `strings.Join(lines, "\n")` with each line padded |
| `strings.Repeat("\n", n)` for blank lines | `theme.EmptyLineBg(width)` |
| `lipgloss.NewStyle().Render(text)` with no background | `.Background(ColorBackground)` mandatory |
| Hardcoded hex color | Global variables (`ColorBackground`, `ColorDim`, etc.) |

`JoinHorizontal`/`JoinVertical` are acceptable **only** if the result is wrapped in a `.Background(ColorBackground).Width(w)` style.

`lipgloss.Place` → always use `WithWhitespaceStyle(lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground))`
(Lip Gloss v2 removed `WithWhitespaceBackground`).

**Safety net, not a replacement (DEVDESK-209).** The router asks the terminal to
use `ColorBackground` as its default background (`tea.View.BackgroundColor`). The
helpers above stay mandatory: the native background is absent in 16-colour
terminals, under `NO_COLOR`, without a TTY, in a terminal or tmux that ignores
OSC 11, and during a `tea.ExecProcess` (the child sees the terminal's own
default). A bare cell there shows the user's background. See
`docs/architecture/app-shell.md`.

**Known gap: the text input's cursor cell.** In Bubbles v2 the virtual cursor
(`textinput.Styles.Cursor`) carries a colour and no background, so that one cell
cannot take `ColorBackground`. `theme.StyleTextInput` sets every other state and
the cursor colour (`ColorHighlight`); the single-cell gap is accepted.

**Drawing over an already rendered screen** (the command palette) goes through
`overlay.Compose` (`internal/ui/overlay`) and nothing else: it splices with
`x/ansi` and never cuts an escape sequence. `lipgloss.Place` stays for full-screen
modals. Never slice a styled line by bytes or runes.

### Rule 117 : Centralized helpers of the `theme` package

**Never recreate `bg()`, `padWithBg()`, `bgWrap()` locally.**

| Function | Usage |
|----------|-------|
| `theme.Bg(s)` | Plain text with the app background |
| `theme.PadWithBg(content, width)` | Pad up to `width` with background |
| `theme.BgLine(s, width)` | Text + background + pad up to `width` |
| `theme.BgWrap(s, width)` | Background + pad on each line (multi-line) |
| `theme.EmptyLineBg(width)` | Blank line filled with background |
| `theme.OverlayBoxStyle()` | Standard style for overlay modals |
| `overlay.Compose(base, box, x, y, width)` | Box drawn over rendered lines, ANSI-safe |

- **Inline text** → `theme.Bg("text")`
- **Full line** → `theme.BgLine("text", width)`
- **Multi-line paragraph** → `theme.BgWrap(text, width)`
- **Blank line** → `theme.EmptyLineBg(width)`
- **Modal overlay** → `theme.OverlayBoxStyle().Render(content)`

### Rule 118 : Standardizing table and tab colors

| Element | Foreground | Background |
|---------|-----------|------------|
| Table header | `ColorSecondary` | — |
| Selected row (normal) | **each column's own** | `ColorTableLineSelected`, bold |
| Selected row (error) | `ColorBlack` | `ColorError` |
| Active tab | `ColorBlack` | `ColorSecondary` |
| Inactive tab | `ColorDim` | `ColorCommandLineBg` |

**Selected row (normal)** (§3.72 in the backlog; confirmed 2026-09-21). It used to
be one flat `ColorBlack` on `ColorSecondary`, dropping every column's own
colour — see Rule 122's "Selected row" section for why that used to be
mandatory and why it no longer is for this one variant: every cell now
repaints `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold **itself**, which is what makes
keeping the per-cell foreground safe instead of a return of the defect.
`error`, `busy` (`TableStylesForState`) and severity
(`TableStylesForSeverity`) are untouched — a solid background there still
means "this whole row is in that state," which per-cell colour would fight.

`ColorTableLineSelected` (`table_line_selected` in a theme file) is its own
key rather than an alias of `ColorSeverityLow`, on purpose: `ColorSeverityLow`
now points at the same tone as `ColorDim` — the colour the `:sec` inventory
already uses for a "0" count (Rule 122's "Color discipline") — so a theme
tuning "how muted is a LOW finding" no longer also retunes the selection
highlight by coincidence. Both keys default to the same hex the "normal"
selection has always used, so nothing changes on screen from this split by
itself.

Mandatory centralized functions:
- `theme.DefaultTableStyles()` — base style
- `theme.TableStylesForState(state)` — `"normal"` or `"error"`
- `theme.TableStylesForSeverity(severity)` — `"CRITICAL"`, `"HIGH"`, `"MEDIUM"`, `"LOW"`, `"UNKNOWN"`

Forbidden:
- ❌ Selection styles defined locally in views
- ❌ `ColorPrimary` for active tabs or headers (use `ColorSecondary`)

### Rule 119 : No hardcoded hex color outside `colors.go`

**A hex literal (`lipgloss.Color("#...")`, `color.RGBA{…}`) must appear ONLY in `internal/ui/theme/colors.go`.**

One exemption: the body of `DefaultTheme` in `internal/ui/theme/manager.go`, the embedded default theme. `TestGuardNoHexColorOutsideColorsGo` (`internal/ui/theme/source_guard_test.go`) enforces both. The invalid-field underline colour is `theme.ColorInvalidField`, an alias (Rule 140).

Palette variables are `color.Color` (`image/color`), not a Lip Gloss type. Read
one back with `theme.Hex(c)` (`#rrggbb`). A theme file is validated on load:
`theme.LoadTheme` refuses the whole file when a non-empty colour is not `#rgb`
or `#rrggbb` (see `docs/architecture/configuration.md`).

3-level architecture:

| Level | File | Role |
|--------|---------|------|
| **1. Base palette** | `colors.go` lines 6-32 | Raw hex colors (Catppuccin) |
| **2. Semantic colors** | `colors.go` lines 34+ | Aliases by usage, referencing the palette |
| **3. Styles** | `styles.go`, views | lipgloss styles using the semantic colors |

If a hex color is needed with no semantic equivalent:
1. Add it to the base palette (`colors.go`, hex section)
2. Create a semantic alias that references the palette

```go
// ✅ CORRECT
var ColorMaroon = lipgloss.Color("#eba0ac")  // in the base palette
ColorSeverityHigh = ColorMaroon              // in the semantic section

// ❌ WRONG
ColorSeverityHigh = lipgloss.Color("#eba0ac")  // hardcoded hex in the semantic section
```

`manager.go`'s fallbacks → reference `colors.go`, never hex values.

### Rule 127 : Relative time — `theme.TimeAgo`

**Every view displaying a relative time must use `theme.TimeAgo(t time.Time) string`** (`internal/ui/theme/timeago.go`).

| Duration | Output |
|-------|--------|
| < 1 min | `"now"` |
| < 1 hour | `"59 min ago"` |
| < 24 h | `"23 hr ago"` |
| < 30 days | `"30 days ago"` |
| < 12 months | `"11 mo ago"` |
| else | `"99 yr ago"` |
| zero | `""` |

Forbidden: local implementations, long formats, compact with no space.

### Rule 129 : Interface and log language — English US only

**All UI text and all logs must be in American English.**

| Category | Rule |
|-----------|-------|
| Labels, titles, UI messages | ✅ English US |
| Error messages (footer) | ✅ English US |
| Help (`GetHelpContent`, `GetShortcuts`) | ✅ English US |
| Cell values, empty messages | ✅ English US |
| Logs (`log.Printf`) | ✅ English US |
| Code comments | ✅ English only (Rule 307) |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT
m.footerStatus = "Loading workspaces..."
m.footerError = "Failed to refresh — check logs"

// ❌ WRONG
m.footerStatus = "Chargement des workspaces..."
m.footerError = "Échec du rafraîchissement — voir les logs"
```

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

## Code quality rules and proactive checks

### Rule 301 : Systematic code quality check before commit

**MANDATORY**: Before creating a commit, ALWAYS perform the following checks:

#### 1. Go linter (golangci-lint)
```bash
golangci-lint run
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix ALL warnings and errors
- ✅ Specifically check deprecation warnings (SA1019)
- ✅ NEVER ignore warnings without documented justification

#### 2. Tests
```bash
go test ./...
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that all tests pass
- ✅ If tests fail, fix them BEFORE the commit

#### 3. Build
```bash
go build
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that the build succeeds without errors
- ✅ Test the application if functional changes were made

#### 4. Deprecated dependencies

**Detection:**
- Check golangci-lint SA1019 warnings
- Look in go.mod for packages marked as deprecated

**Action:**
- Replace IMMEDIATELY with a maintained alternative
- Document the replacement in the commit message
- Update the documentation (.claude/CLAUDE.md)

**Examples of common replacements:**
- `github.com/go-ping/ping` → `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing`

### Rule 302 : IDE diagnostics check

**MANDATORY**: Before each commit, check the IDE diagnostics:

```
Use mcp__ide__getDiagnostics to check:
- Compilation errors
- Unused parameters
- Unused imports
- Other warnings
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Fix or justify every diagnostic
- ✅ Do not ignore "unused parameter" without a reason

### Rule 303 : go.mod and dependencies

**After any dependency change:**

```bash
go mod tidy
go mod verify
```

**Required actions:**
- ✅ Verify that go.mod is up to date
- ✅ Verify that go.sum is consistent
- ✅ Document new dependencies in .claude/CLAUDE.md

### Rule 304 : Quality commit message

**Mandatory format for quality fixes — in English (see Rule 307):**

```
type: short description

Detailed description explaining:
- What was detected (warning, error, etc.)
- Why it was a problem
- How it was resolved

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

**Commit types for quality:**
- `fix:` - Bug fix detected by linter
- `chore:` - Deprecated dependency replacement
- `refactor:` - Code quality improvement

### Rule 305 : MANDATORY pre-commit checklist

**Before EVERY commit, check:**

- [ ] `golangci-lint run` → 0 warnings
- [ ] `go test ./...` → PASS
- [ ] `go build` → SUCCESS
- [ ] `mcp__ide__getDiagnostics` → No critical error
- [ ] `go.mod` up to date (if dependencies changed)
- [ ] Documentation updated (if API changed)
- [ ] Tests added (if new feature)

**If EVEN ONE of these checks fails:**
- ❌ DO NOT create the commit
- ✅ Fix it first
- ✅ Restart the checklist

### Rule 306 : MANDATORY proactivity

**Claude Code MUST:**
- ✅ Check the linter WITHOUT the user asking
- ✅ Propose fixes BEFORE the commit
- ✅ Flag deprecated dependencies AS SOON AS they are detected
- ✅ Document all quality changes

**Claude Code MUST NEVER:**
- ❌ Wait for the user to flag a warning
- ❌ Create a commit with unresolved warnings
- ❌ Ignore dependency issues
- ❌ Forget to update the documentation

### Correct workflow examples

**Example 1 - Feature commit:**
```
1. Write the code
2. go build → verify compilation
3. golangci-lint run → fix warnings
4. go test ./... → verify tests
5. mcp__ide__getDiagnostics → check the IDE
6. git commit with a detailed message
```

**Example 2 - Detecting a deprecated dependency:**
```
1. golangci-lint detects SA1019
2. Look up the recommended alternative
3. Replace the import and the code
4. go mod tidy
5. Test that everything works
6. Update .claude/CLAUDE.md
7. git commit explaining the replacement
```

### Rule 307 : Commits and code comments — English only

**Every git commit message and every comment in the code must be written
in English**, regardless of the language used to converse with the user.

| Element | Language |
|---------|--------|
| Commit message (title + body) | ✅ English only |
| Code comment (`//`, `/* */`, docstring) | ✅ English only |
| Replies to the user in the conversation | The user's language (see memory `feedback-langue-francais`) |
| UI and logs (Rule 129) | English US only — already covered, unchanged |

This **replaces** the earlier tolerance listed in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` under
"Code Conventions" ("Comments: French or English both accepted"): existing
French comments are not to be rewritten wholesale, but any new comment and
any edit to an existing comment must be in English.

// ❌ WRONG (a French comment, which Rule 307 forbids)
// on relance avec un backoff car l'API limite les rafales au-delà de 10 req/s

Title: "Diagnostics Tab — Tracing the path",
				Body: "Traces the hops between this machine and a target, in this process — no " +
					"container, no traceroute binary. Native Linux and WSL2 only: on macOS, Windows and WSL1 the Trace Path button, H, " +
					"enter and ctrl+o are greyed out, and the footer says why. IPv4 only: a host name is resolved to its IPv4 address. " +
					"The column starts on this machine: the interface the target's traffic leaves by, " +
					"with its source address, and the gateway, read from this machine's routing table, " +
					"then the hops. Under WSL2 the source row names the WSL2 VM, and in NAT mode the " +
					"first hop through the virtual switch is labelled Windows host.\n\n" +
					"The target is the one typed in the Diagnostics form, or the host of the results; a " +
					"port is ignored because the trace probes a host, not a service. Press enter in the trace to start it, or to trace again. Each hop is a UDP datagram sent to UDP " +
					"port 33435 with a growing time-to-live; the router that drops it answers, and the " +
					"table fills in as the answers come. No connection is made. Nothing is sent before you " +
					"press enter.\n\n" +
					"A silent hop is not a failure: many routers do not answer these probes, so the row " +
					"reads silent and the trace goes on. The header says how a trace ended.\n\n" +
					"When the target never answers, the silent hops at the end fold into one row, " +
					"no response beyond hop N, and the last hop that answered reads last to answer. " +
					"When this machine has no route to the target, the interface row reads no route " +
					"and nothing is sent; undetermined means the routing table could not be read, " +
					"which says nothing either way. DevDesk shows only what came back: it does not " +
					"say why the rest stayed silent.\n\n" +

content.content:
- **Four exceptions, declared** in `keymap.DeclaredExceptions()`: `o` (open
  the pipeline the forge resolves, security/results/ci-tab), `ctrl+y` (copy
  the `docker run` command), `ctrl+o` (write the chosen base images into
  the Dockerfiles, security/results/remediation-tab) and `ctrl+o` again on
  netdiag/path and netdiag/trace (open the "Trace from" selector: this
  machine or a running container; it changes nothing by itself). Burning a global
  uppercase letter for an action present in a single sub-screen would cost
  more than it gains. They are written up as exceptions so the next survey
  does not mistake them for drift. `ctrl+o` is nano's Write Out, and the
`o` (`openPipelineKey`) becomes checkable rather than merely tidy.

Two limits, both deliberate. `↑↓`, `enter/esc`, `tab / shift+tab` are display
strings with no counterpart to compare against — a test that guessed would
report the 52 help labels the naive version does, and Rule 138 keeps most of
them off the screen anyway. And the granularity is the **package**, not the
view's state: a key bound in one tab and announced in another passes. What these
catch is the key bound *nowhere*, which is what both instances were.

**`ctrl+o` on `netdiag/path` (DEVDESK-330).** A declared Ctrl exception
(`keymap.DeclaredExceptions()`, key `ctrl+o`, surface `netdiag/path`; the
`security/results/remediation-tab` entry for the same key is a separate one, so
the pair is keyed by key and surface). It opens the "Trace from" selector (this
machine or a running Docker Engine container) and changes nothing by itself,
unlike the remediation tab's `ctrl+o`, which writes files. The target field has
the keyboard in `pathEditing`, so no bare letter is free there; `textinput` does

taken against a real podman; `TestTheTwoTemplateSetsAreStillUnmeasured` fails
  the day the two sets stop matching, so a divergence is recorded deliberately.
- **`system df -v` is scraped, not templated**, and is therefore disabled under
  podman (`Shape.ParsesSystemDFVerbose`). It is a fixed-width table read at
  offsets taken from its header line, and there is no `--format` that exposes
  per-image unique size.

- **Four typed, read-only reads for the Path tab** (`container_network.go`,
  DEVDESK-330, DEVDESK-331), each with a `context.Context` that kills the
  invocation: `InspectContainerNetworking(ctx, id)`, `ListContainersContext(ctx,
  all)` (`ListContainers(all)` is unchanged and does not use it),
  `EngineOperatingSystem(ctx)` and `InspectNetworkBridge(ctx, networkID)`. They
  run `container inspect`, `ps`, `info` and `network inspect` and nothing else. `InspectContainerNetworking` runs
Trivy, cosign, the netdiag image — are pulled by their `run` and are **not**
verified: a declared exception.

## Network Diagnostics View

`internal/ui/netdiag/` — five tabs:
- **Diagnostics tab** (`model.go`): target, port and resolver, then
  `internal/netcheck`'s pipeline — resolve, route, reach, connect, TLS, HTTP —
  chained one stage per message so the footer can name the question being asked.
  The seven tool checkboxes are gone (§3.33): the checks follow from the target
  and from what has already failed.
  **The route stage** (`netcheck/stage_route.go`, DEVDESK-474, D151) sorts each
  lookup error with `nettrace.IsNoRoute`: a proven absence of route is a finding,
  any other failure proves nothing (D20). Only the first 8 resolved addresses
  (`maxRoutedAddresses`) are looked up. The verdict:
  - every address proven without a route: **Fail** (`<host> has no local route`);
  - none routed and at least one undetermined: **Unknown**;
  - some routed and at least one proven without a route: **Warn**,
    `partial-route`; only the proven addresses are counted, and undetermined ones
    are added as `route undetermined for N`;
  - some routed, none proven, at least one undetermined: **OK**,
    `route-undetermined`.

  The system's error text (in the machine's language) appears only in the facts
  `No route` and `Route undetermined`, never in the summary (Rule 129). In the
  Fail case the results header and the MCP verdict read FAIL, where they read
  UNKNOWN before.

  Real coverage is Linux and WSL2 only. `go-netroute` returns a
  `windows.Errno` that `IsNoRoute` does not recognize on Windows, and an error
  with no errno on macOS: both end as `undetermined`, which is the safe side.
  Two limits to know: if `go-netroute` stopped wrapping the netlink errno with
  `%w`, Linux would fall back to `undetermined` silently, with no failing
  build; and `prohibit` routes (`EACCES`) stay `undetermined`. Windows and macOS
  support is a follow-up story, to be created (see D151 in `docs/backlog.md`).
- **Ports tab** (`ports_model.go`): the machine's own socket table, re-read
  every `ports_refresh_interval`, filtered by protocol, state and text. `K`
  terminates a process, after a confirmation. It runs **no container** — see
  `internal/ports` below. Column 0 is the activity column (DEVDESK-150, below).
- **Interfaces tab** (`interfaces_model.go`): this machine's network interfaces
  — name, state, MTU, MAC, RX/TX error counters, addresses — in a `datatable`.
  It runs **no container**; see `internal/netiface` below. It was the Topology
  tab, and §3.44 is why three of its four sections are gone rather than
  translated.
- **Forward tab** (`forward_model.go`, `forward_form.go`): the port
  redirections, `N` to open one, `space` to pause or resume it and `K` to delete
  it. It holds **no listener** — see `internal/forward` below.
- **Path tab** (`path_model.go`, `path_view.go`, `path_run.go`,
  `path_target.go`, `path_from_route.go`, `path_steps.go`; DEVDESK-328,
  DEVDESK-329): the hop-by-hop path to
  a target, from `internal/nettrace` (below). It is the fifth and last tab
  (`tabPath = 4`, `tabCount = 5`). It runs **no container**; since DEVDESK-330 it
  can name a running Docker Engine container as the source of the column (below),
  but the probes still leave from this machine. Three states:
  `pathEditing` (the target field has the keyboard), `pathRunning` (field
  blurred, hops arriving) and `pathDone` (hops kept on screen). The **body is
  always the hop table** (`PathModel.view()` returns `table.View()`, Rule 139),
  in every state: columns Hop, Step, Address, RTT, with a silent hop dim and
  never red. **The column starts on this machine** (DEVDESK-329): three local
  rows, then the hops. `source` reads `this machine`; `interface` reads

  rows, then the hops. `source` reads `this machine`; `interface` reads
  `<name> (<source address>)`; `gateway` reads the gateway address. The local
  rows have an empty Hop and RTT (they asked nobody; `-` means "no answer") and
  the default text colour. `pathSteps` (`path_steps.go`) is the only place that
  orders the rows; the table item is a `pathStep` (kind source, interface,
  gateway or hop; DEVDESK-330 adds container, network and trace, below).
  Nothing is shown before the route is known, so a resolution
  error leaves 0 rows. The **target field is not in the body**: it sits in the footer's
  bar slot, framed by `components.BarFrame` (`Target › ` + the field,
  placeholder `hostname or IPv4 address`). That slot is shown on this
  tab in every state, so `GetFooterHeight()` is 5 (bar 2, tab row 1, blank
  line 1, info line 1) and the layout does not move between editing, running
  and done. The tab keeps its own `FooterMessage`, returned by `activeFooter`,
  so `WantsBlink()` follows a running trace. `Model.Running()` is true while a
  trace runs, so the router does not rebuild the view mid-trace.

  Keys: `enter` launches (while editing) or traces again (when done); `esc`
  cancels a running trace, and returns a finished one to editing with the
  value kept; `tab` switches tab; `up`, `down`, `pgup`, `pgdown`, `home` and
  `end` move in the table in every state. While editing, `esc`, `tab` and
  `shift+tab` do nothing in the field. A paste reaches the field only while
  editing (Rule 111). A changed field value clears the persistent error.
  `ctrl+o` opens the "Trace from" selector in `pathEditing` and `pathDone`; while
  a trace runs it warns `A path trace is running — esc cancels it`, and where the
  trace is unsupported it warns with the platform reason (`sourceChoosable`, the
  one answer the header and the handler both read). While the selector is open it
  holds every key: `up`, `down`, `pgup`, `pgdown`, `home` and `end` move, `enter`
  chooses, `esc` closes, and every other key is swallowed, `tab` and `shift+tab`
  included (`netdiag.Model.Update` hands the key to the Path model before the tab
  switch). A paste is dropped. `PathModel.InEditMode()` is true while it is open,
  so `q` and `:` reach the view and do not quit or open the palette.
------
- **A periodic refresh never blinks**: `SetItems` leaves `busy` alone, so a
  refresh with nothing busy leaves column 0 empty and `WantsBlink()` false; one
  during a kill keeps the dots and the cursor.
- **A failed network test is not a row operation.** The Diagnostics table keeps
  its result in the Verdict column; no `⊗` was added (open question 4 of the
  activity-indicator stories, option A). The Diagnostics and Interfaces tables
  have no `Indicator`; neither does the Path tab's hop table (DEVDESK-328): a
  trace is one run, not a per-row operation, and its running state is the
  footer's shared dot. The Path files `path_model.go`, `path_target.go` and
  `path_view.go` (and, since DEVDESK-329, `path_steps.go`; since DEVDESK-330,
  `path_source.go`, `path_container.go`, `path_source_picker.go` and
-----
choosing a source goes back to `pathReady` with the target kept and sends
nothing; `esc` cancels a running trace, then goes back to `traceOrigin` with
fields, focus, filter and results untouched (no `resetToForm`); navigation moves
the table. An open selector holds every key, `tab` included. `tab` and
`shift+tab` otherwise still switch tabs, so the sub-level survives a visit to
another tab. `traceShortcuts()` is the one constructor of the sub-level's
shortcuts: ready and done share one key set (Rule 130), the selector and a
running trace replace the list. `InEditMode()` is true in the sub-level only
while the selector is open.

The Path tab still exists at this step and shares `m.pathModel`; its removal is
the next step of DEVDESK-471.

**Files.** `trace_form.go` holds what the form does: `traceable()` (the one
availability, read by the button, the header and the handler, Rule 130),
`traceFromForm()` (the `enter` handler), the target validation and
`traceUnusedNotice`. `trace_level.go` holds the sub-level: `startFromForm`,
`ready`, `openTrace`, `inTrace`, `handleKeyTrace`, `escFromTrace` (with
`restoreFormFocus`), `traceTitle` and `traceShortcuts`.

**Order of refusals in `traceFromForm`.** An unsupported platform
(`launchable()`, macOS, Windows, WSL1) comes first: the button is greyed and
the reason is in the footer. Then a trace already running (`reasonPathBusy`).
Then the target.

**Target validation (Rule 140).** The target goes through `parsePathTarget`,
the parser of the Path tab, so an empty, invalid, `host:port` or IPv6 value
gets the same sentence as on the Path tab (first letter capitalized). The
failure is carried twice: the Target field is underlined
(`traceMarks`, `InvalidMarks.Sync`, from `Update()` only) and the error sits
in the footer at level Error, derived from `traceValidation.Status()` in
`statusLine()`. Nothing is invalid before the first refused `enter` on the
button; after that, every edit of the Target revalidates (`revalidateTrace`).
`enter` on a text field still runs the diagnostics and does not validate
the trace target.

**Port and DNS Server.** The trace probes the path to a host, so both fields
are ignored. When either holds a non-blank value, `traceUnusedNotice` posts an
Info notice on the Path model's footer (`Port is not used by the path trace`,
`DNS Server is not used by the path trace`, or both). It is posted after
`startFromForm`, because launching clears that footer. The values stay in the
form.

**Coupling with the Path tab.** The sub-level has no model of its own: it
drives `m.pathModel`. Starting from the form therefore overwrites the Path
tab's field (`prefill`) and its previous run, and the trace shows on both: the
Path tab sees the same hops, and `esc` there cancels the same run. Going back
to the form does not clear the Path model. This coupling disappears when the
Path tab is removed (P2-02).

**What is configurable, and what is not.** `internal/netcheck` held its timeouts
as constants with a comment saying they would become settings when somebody
asked; `network:` is what they became.

| Setting | Replaces |
|---|---|
| `check_timeout` | five per-stage constants — 5 s for DNS and the dial, 8 s for TLS and HTTP, 4 s for the ping |
| `ping_count` | `pingCount` |
| `cert_expiry_warn_days` | `expiryWarnWindow` |
| `ports_refresh_interval` | the 2 s tick |

**One timeout replaces five**, and the default is the old *maximum* so nothing
that answers today starts failing. The 5 / 5 / 8 / 8 / 4 split was never argued
anywhere — five rows for one idea, and each of the five a separate guess. The
cost is stated rather than discovered: an unreachable host now spends 8 s on DNS
instead of 5, which the staged progress line makes legible rather than a hang.

`traceroute_max_hops` was a sixth setting and went with the trace it bounded
(§3.47). It stays removed: the trace is back in the process (DEVDESK-327, see
[The path trace](#the-path-trace--internalnettrace)), but `nettrace.Options.MaxHops`
is not wired to any setting, and the Path tab (DEVDESK-328) still traces with
the engine's defaults (`nettrace.Options{}`).

Two things stay hardcoded, each for a reason:

- **`MinVersion: VersionTLS10`** — the handshake is *probing*, not securing.

choosing a source goes back to `pathReady` with the target kept and sends
nothing; `esc` cancels a running trace, then goes back to `traceOrigin` with

the table. An open selector holds every key, `tab` included. `tab` and
`shift+tab` otherwise still switch tabs, so the sub-level survives a visit to
another tab. `traceShortcuts()` is the one constructor of the sub-level's
shortcuts: ready and done share one key set (Rule 130), the selector and a
running trace replace the list. `InEditMode()` is true in the sub-level only
while the selector is open.

the next step of DEVDESK-471.

availability, read by the button, the header and the handler, Rule 130),

`restoreFormFocus`), `traceTitle` and `traceShortcuts`.

(`launchable()`, macOS, Windows, WSL1) comes first: the button is greyed and
the reason is in the footer. Then a trace already running (`reasonPathBusy`).

the parser of the Path tab, so an empty, invalid, `host:port` or IPv6 value
gets the same sentence as on the Path tab (first letter capitalized). The
failure is carried twice: the Target field is underlined

to the form does not clear the Path model. This coupling disappears when the
Path tab is removed (P2-02).

as constants with a comment saying they would become settings when somebody
asked; `network:` is what they became.

|---|---|

| `ping_count` | `pingCount` |

anywhere — five rows for one idea, and each of the five a separate guess. The
cost is stated rather than discovered: an unreachable host now spends 8 s on DNS
instead of 5, which the staged progress line makes legible rather than a hang.

is not wired to any setting, and the Path tab (DEVDESK-328) still traces with
the engine's defaults (`nettrace.Options{}`).

- **`MinVersion: VersionTLS10`** — the handshake is *probing*, not securing.

## The Path tab — streaming, cancellation, resolution

How `internal/ui/netdiag` drives `nettrace` (DEVDESK-328).

**Streaming.** `launch` (called from `Update`) creates the run's context, a
buffered `chan tea.Msg` and the launch Cmd: a batch of the producer
- **Generation (`wslenv.DetectKind`, DEVDESK-334).** `ClassifyKind(Facts)`
  returns `KindNone`, `KindWSL1` or `KindWSL2`, reading only `WSL_DISTRO_NAME`
  and the osrelease (`GatherKernel`: no process, no interface listing, nothing
  off Linux). WSL1 is an osrelease containing `Microsoft`, case-sensitive; it is
  checked before the case-insensitive WSL test. The Path tab uses it to refuse
  WSL1 (see "`Supported()` and the Path tab"). `ClassifyKind` can say WSL2 for an
  old 4.19 kernel where `Classify().WSL2` is false; known, minor.
- **Mode.** `wslinfo --networking-mode`, run only under WSL, from
  `/usr/bin/wslinfo` then `/usr/sbin/wslinfo` (absolute paths, never the search
`ErrNotIPv4`, `ErrNotUnicast`, `ErrNoRoute` (`No route to <host> from this
machine — no probe was sent`; matched with `nettrace.IsNoRoute`, which also
accepts a raw `ENETUNREACH` / `EHOSTUNREACH` in the error chain) and `ErrUnsupported` to their own sentence, and
anything else to `The path trace failed — check logs`. The raw error text
(errno, resolver message, in the machine's language) goes to the log only
(`ERROR [netdiag/path] resolve|trace <host>: …`). An error returns the tab to
`pathEditing` with the field focused, the hops cleared and the label shown as a
persistent error (level Error) until the field changes or the next launch.
`handleDoneError` decides what stays on screen: when `nettrace.IsNoRoute(err)`
is true, the column **keeps the local rows** (container rows, source, interface
and gateway, platform labels), with the route set to `pathRoute{NoRoute: true}`

(important for round-robin DNS names, where two independent lookups can
  return different addresses).

### The Trace Path button

The form has two buttons, **Run Diagnostics** and **Trace Path**. `↑` and `↓`
move from the fields to the buttons. `enter` on a text field still runs the
diagnostics, so nobody has to walk to a button first.

Trace Path opens a level of the Diagnostics tab, `Network › Path › <target>`,
with the same table as the [Path tab](#the-path-tab--internalnettrace)
(Hop, Step, Address, RTT). The trace starts when you press the button, from
this machine, and nothing is sent before. `esc` cancels a running trace; `esc`
again returns to the form, with Target, Port and DNS Server as you left them.
The level has no `enter` and no `ctrl+o`: to trace again, go back to the form.
Every key except the table's navigation (and `Tab`, which switches tab) is
ignored there.

The trace probes the path to a host, not a service, so Port and DNS Server
play no part in it. If either is filled, the footer says so and the trace goes
ahead. The Target follows the Path tab's rules: a host name or an IPv4
address, no port, no IPv6. A refused target is underlined and the footer
gives the reason. Where the trace cannot run (macOS, Windows, WSL1) the button
is greyed out and the footer says why.

The level shares its trace with the Path tab, which stays in place for now: a
trace started from the form also appears there.

## The Ports tab — `internal/ports`

The socket table lists this machine's TCP and UDP sockets and the process
holding each, read directly in-process via `gopsutil`. No new dependency was
needed — `gopsutil/v4/net` was already used elsewhere for host metrics.
Windows reads through `iphlpapi`, Linux through `/proc`, and macOS/BSD
shell out to `lsof` — a subprocess, but one the operating system itself
supplies, replacing what used to be a privileged container.
is privileged). A name outside `.localhost` doesn't resolve, and a client with
its own resolver isn't covered. The proxy adds no CORS header: it makes nothing
reachable that wasn't already on the loopback. The proxy binds IPv4 only, and
browsers on Windows and macOS haven't been measured yet.

## The Path tab — `internal/nettrace`

The Path tab shows the hops between this machine and a target, in this
process: nothing runs in a container, there is no `traceroute` binary and no
privilege. It replaces the
container trace that was removed because it answered for the Docker VM and not
for this machine.

- **Native Linux and WSL2 only.** On macOS, native Windows and WSL1 the tab
  opens, `enter` and `ctrl+o` are greyed out, and the footer says why, for
  example `The path trace needs Linux — not available on macOS`. On Windows and
  checks.
- **Nothing is sent before `enter`.** `esc` cancels a running trace and keeps
  the hops already seen. The header says how a trace ended: `Reached at hop N`,
  `Reported unreachable at hop N`, `No answer from the target within N hops`,
  `Stopped after 30 s` or `Canceled`.
- **From Diagnostics.** On the results, `H` on the **Local route** row opens the
  Path tab with the host filled in, without starting the trace.

There is no setting for the maximum number of hops (`traceroute_max_hops`
stays removed): the trace uses the engine's defaults.
| `enter` | A text field or Run Diagnostics | Run the checks |
| `enter` | Trace Path button | Trace the path to the target, in the `Network › Path › <target>` level |
| `esc` | Trace level, while it runs | Cancel the trace and keep the hops already seen |
| `enter` | Trace level, ready or done | Start the trace, or trace again |
| `ctrl+o` | Trace level | Choose where the trace starts (this machine or a running container); choosing starts nothing |
| `H` | Diagnostics results, Local route row | Open the trace level on the target, ready to start; nothing is sent until `enter` |
| `esc` | Trace level, once it is done or before it started | Back to the form or the results it was opened from, with everything kept |
| `↑` `↓` `PageUp` `PageDown` `Home` `End` | Trace level | Move in the hop table |
| `Tab` | Anywhere in net, except while the filter bar is being edited or the Path tab's source selector is open | Switch tab |

`enter` on a text field always runs the diagnostics; only the Trace Path
button traces. In the trace level, every other key is ignored. `H` is greyed out, with the
reason in the footer, on a platform that cannot trace or a target the trace
refuses.

The Target must be a host name or an IPv4 address, with no port. An empty,
invalid, `host:port` or IPv6 target is refused: the field is underlined and the
footer gives the reason, the same wording as the Path tab. Port and DNS Server
do not apply to a trace: if either is filled, the footer says it is ignored.
The button is greyed out on a platform that cannot trace (macOS, Windows,
WSL1), and the footer gives the reason.

## Network Diagnostics — Path tab

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `enter` | Trace the path to the host typed in the target field, or trace again once a trace is done |
| `esc` | While a trace runs: cancel it and keep the hops already seen. Once it is done: edit the target again (the value is kept) |
| `↑` `↓` `PageUp` `PageDown` `Home` `End` | Move in the hop table |
| `Tab` | Switch tab |

The field takes a host name or an IPv4 address, with no port: `host:80` is
refused (`Path ignores ports: enter a host or IP address only`). Nothing is
sent until you press `enter`. `enter` is greyed out on a platform that cannot trace (the trace runs on Linux
only, for now).

From the Diagnostics tab, `H` on the **Local route** row of the results opens
the Path tab with that target's host already in the field. It does not start a
trace; press `enter` there. On any other row `H` is greyed out. If a trace is
already running, `H` only switches to the Path tab.

## Lowercase — local filters and toggles, view by view

Lowercase letters never modify anything; they're local and can repeat
across views. Examples: `r`/`p`/`s`/`t`/`z` in Containers are cumulative
state filters; `c`/`h`/`m`/`l` in Security are cumulative severity filters;
`t`/`u`/`l`/`e`/`n`/`z` in Network Diagnostics filter protocol/state (Ports tab); `g` in

(Hop, Step, Address, RTT). The trace starts when you press the button, from
this machine, and nothing is sent before. `esc` cancels a running trace; `esc`
again returns to the form, with Target, Port and DNS Server as you left them.
The level has no `enter` and no `ctrl+o`: to trace again, go back to the form.
Every key except the table's navigation (and `Tab`, which switches tab) is
ignored there.

The trace probes the path to a host, not a service, so Port and DNS Server
play no part in it. If either is filled, the footer says so and the trace goes
ahead. The Target follows the Path tab's rules: a host name or an IPv4
address, no port, no IPv6. A refused target is underlined and the footer
gives the reason. Where the trace cannot run (macOS, Windows, WSL1) the button
is greyed out and the footer says why.

The level shares its trace with the Path tab, which stays in place for now: a
trace started from the form also appears there.

## The Ports tab — `internal/ports`

The socket table lists this machine's TCP and UDP sockets and the process
holding each, read directly in-process via `gopsutil`. No new dependency was
needed — `gopsutil/v4/net` was already used elsewhere for host metrics.
Windows reads through `iphlpapi`, Linux through `/proc`, and macOS/BSD
shell out to `lsof` — a subprocess, but one the operating system itself
supplies, replacing what used to be a privileged container.

its own resolver isn't covered. The proxy adds no CORS header: it makes nothing
reachable that wasn't already on the loopback. The proxy binds IPv4 only, and
browsers on Windows and macOS haven't been measured yet.

## The Path tab — `internal/nettrace`

The Path tab shows the hops between this machine and a target, in this
process: nothing runs in a container, there is no `traceroute` binary and no
privilege. It replaces the
container trace that was removed because it answered for the Docker VM and not
for this machine.

  `Stopped after 30 s` or `Canceled`.
- **From Diagnostics.** On the results, `H` on the **Local route** row opens the
  Path tab with the host filled in, without starting the trace.

stays removed): the trace uses the engine's defaults.

26	- Multi-context configuration management via YAML
27	- Local workspaces management with git metadata
28	- Claude Code session list (`:agent-usage` / `:au`): sessions found on this machine, by project and date, and per session the agent tree (orchestrator and sub-agents: types, models, tokens, share of the total; sortable by Total; also per agent a state (running / idle / done / unknown, idle after 5 min without a transcript line) shown as a status dot in the first column (the `running` dot blinks, DEVDESK-151) and as text, tool calls and duration; and an indicative cost per agent, `Est. cost` (orange from 75 % and red from 90 % of the session's estimated cost, when at least two agents are priced), from prices you write in the context YAML (`agent_usage.prices`, none shipped), with the session's `Billed` cost and `Unattributed` in the header, DEVDESK-47; a `Breakdown` colour bar per agent and, with `tab` inside a session, a Breakdown tab splitting the whole session's tokens by category, model and agent, as a percentage of tokens, DEVDESK-98). An open session updates live: read again every 2 s while active, only what was appended; paused after 5 min with no write and no unfinished sub-agent, when its transcript is gone, or while the terminal is not focused (header `Updates › paused`, then `paused (terminal not focused)`; `app.when_unfocused: run` keeps it live); `ctrl+r` reads it again in full. The sessions list itself is not live.

32	Tasks live in `mise.toml` — there is no Makefile. `mise tasks` lists them all.
